solution:
The degree of dissociation is given by \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_b / c}\). Here,

\(K_b = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\); \(c = 0.01 = 1 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{M}\)

Hence, \(\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{1.8 \times 10^{-5}}{1 \times 10^{-2}}} = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(= \sqrt{18 \times 10^{-4}} = 4.243 \times 10^{-2} = 0.04243\)

[Textbook misprint: the book writes the temperature-dependence relation with \(2.303\,RT\) in the denominator, where \(2.303\,R\) belongs: the temperature is already carried by the bracket \((T_2 - T_1)/T_1T_2\). The chapter's own Eq. (6.23) prints \(E_a/(2.303\,R)\), and this example's own substitution divides by \(2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}}\) with no \(T\), which is what gives its printed \(2.212\). The formula has been corrected here; the printed answer \(1.464 \times 10^{5}\) min is correct.]

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)

Rate constants at two different temperatures, \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) respectively, and the corresponding half lives \((t_{1/2})_1\) and \((t_{1/2})_2\).

\((t_{1/2})_1 = \dfrac{0.693}{k_1}\) and \((t_{1/2})_2 = \dfrac{0.693}{k_2}\)

Hence, \(\dfrac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\)

The equation, \(\log_{10}\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R} \times \left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right]\)

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right]\)

\(E_a = 250\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), \(T_1 = 720\ \mathrm{K}\),

\(T_2 = 820\ \mathrm{K}\), \((t_{1/2})_2 = 900\) min

Thus, \(\log_{10}\dfrac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \dfrac{250 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}}{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}}}\left[\dfrac{820\ \mathrm{K} - 720\ \mathrm{K}}{820\ \mathrm{K} \times 720\ \mathrm{K}}\right] = 2.212\)

\(\dfrac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \text{antilog } 2.212 = 162.7\)

\((t_{1/2})_1 = (t_{1/2})_2 \times 162.7 = 900 \times 162.7 = 1.464 \times 10^{5}\) min
note: The two half-lives use k1 and k2, printed k for both.

solution:
Given : \([\mathrm{A}]_0 = 20\ \mathrm{mmol\ dm^{-3}}\), \([\mathrm{A}]_t = 8\ \mathrm{mmol\ dm^{-3}}\), \(t = 38\) min, \(t_{1/2} = ?\)

For a first order reaction,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303}{38\ \mathrm{min}}\log_{10}\dfrac{20}{8} = \dfrac{2.303}{38}\log_{10} 2.5\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.3979}{38} = 0.02411\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

(The concentrations may be left in \(\mathrm{mmol\ dm^{-3}}\) because only their ratio is used.)

Hence

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.02411\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}} = 28.7\ \mathrm{min}\)

The half life of the reaction is \(28.7\) minutes.

Going from \(0.8\ \mathrm{M}\) to \(0.2\ \mathrm{M}\) is a fall to one quarter of the initial concentration, and \(\tfrac{1}{4} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\), so exactly two half lives have elapsed.

Since the half life of a first order reaction does not depend on the initial concentration (Eq. 6.10), each of those halvings takes the same time. Hence \(2\,t_{1/2} = 12\ \mathrm{h}\) and \(t_{1/2} = 6\ \mathrm{h}\).

This is confirmed by the integrated rate law: \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{12}\log_{10}\dfrac{0.8}{0.2} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.6021}{12} = 0.1156\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}\), giving \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.1156} = 6\ \mathrm{h}\).

The alternative \(12\ \mathrm{h}\) is the time for the whole change rather than for one halving, \(3\ \mathrm{h}\) would correspond to four half lives and \(1.5\ \mathrm{h}\) to eight, neither of which matches a fall to one quarter.

Given : \(T = 500\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} = 500 + 273 = 773\ \mathrm{K}\), \(k = 1.6 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}\), \(E_a = 56\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} = 56 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J/mol}\), frequency factor \(\mathrm{A} = ?\)

The Arrhenius equation \(k = \mathrm{A}\,e^{-E_a/RT}\) in logarithmic form (Eq. 6.19 converted to base \(10\)) gives

\(\log_{10}\mathrm{A} = \log_{10}k + \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT}\)

\(\dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT} = \dfrac{56 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}}{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}} \times 773\ \mathrm{K}} = \dfrac{56 \times 10^{3}}{14801} = 3.784\)

\(\log_{10}k = \log_{10}(1.6 \times 10^{3}) = 3.204\)

Hence

\(\log_{10}\mathrm{A} = 3.204 + 3.784 = 6.988\)

\(\mathrm{A} = \text{antilog } 6.988 = 9.72 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

The frequency factor is \(9.72 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}\). It carries the same units as \(k\), since the exponential factor is dimensionless.

Arrhenius equation

\(k = \mathrm{A}\,e^{-E_a/RT}\) is written as

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{k} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT}\)

\(E_a = 240\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}} = 240 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\),

\(T = 600\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{A} = 1.6 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

Hence \(\log_{10}\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{k} = \dfrac{240 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}}{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}} \times 600\ \mathrm{K}} = 20.89\)

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{k} = \text{antilog } 20.89 = 7.78 \times 10^{20}\)

and \(k = \dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{7.78 \times 10^{20}} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}{7.78 \times 10^{20}} = 2.057 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

(a) For fcc unit cell, \(r = 0.3535\,a\)

\(r = 144.4\ \mathrm{pm} = 144.4 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m} = 144.4 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm}\)

\(a = \dfrac{r}{0.3535} = \dfrac{144.4 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm}}{0.3535} = 4.085 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\)

(b) Volume of Ag atom \(= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{4}{3} \times 3.142 \times (144.4 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm})^3 = 1.261 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)

(c) In fcc unit cell, there are 4 Ag atoms.

Volume occupied by 4 Ag atoms \(= 4 \times 1.261 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 5.044 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)

Total volume of unit cell \(= a^3 = (4.085 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^3 = 6.817 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)

Percent of volume occupied by Ag atoms \(= \dfrac{\text{volume occupied by atoms in unit cell}}{\text{total volume of unit cell}} \times 100 = \dfrac{5.044 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}}{6.817 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}} \times 100 = 74\%\)

(d) Percent empty space \(= 100 - 74 = 26\%\)
note: The line above gives 1.261e-23; 4 x 1.26 is 5.04, not the 5.044 printed.

solution:
**Step 1: radius of the sphere.** In a simple cubic unit cell the particles are at the corners and touch each other along the edge, so

\(a = 2r\) and hence \(r = \dfrac{a}{2}\)

**Step 2: volume of one sphere.**

\(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \left(\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{\pi a^3}{6}\)

**Step 3: total volume of particles.** A simple cubic unit cell contains only 1 particle, so the volume occupied by particles in the unit cell is \(\dfrac{\pi a^3}{6}\).

**Step 4: packing efficiency.**

\(\text{Packing efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{volume occupied by particles in unit cell}}{\text{total volume of unit cell}} \times 100 = \dfrac{\pi a^3/6}{a^3} \times 100 = \dfrac{100\pi}{6}\)

\(= \dfrac{100 \times \pi}{6} = \mathbf{52.36\%}\)

Thus 52.36 % of the total space in a simple cubic lattice is occupied by particles and 47.64 % is empty (void) space.

[Textbook misprint: in part (ii) the book's printed substitution keeps the \(\times\,2\) carried over from part (i), writing \(0.5 \times 2\) in the numerator. That contradicts the formula printed immediately above it, \(\text{number of unit cells} = x/(\rho a^3)\), which has no factor \(n\), and it also contradicts the book's own printed answer: the expression as printed evaluates to \(3.24 \times 10^{21}\), which is part (i)'s answer, whereas \(0.5/(8.55 \times (3.306 \times 10^{-8})^3) = 1.62 \times 10^{21}\), which is what the book prints. The substitution is corrected below; the printed answers of both parts are correct as they stand.]

i. Number of atoms in \(x\) g niobium \(= \dfrac{xn}{\rho a^3}\)

\(x = 0.5\ \mathrm{g}\), \(n = 2\) (for bcc structure), \(\rho = 8.55\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\),

\(a = 330.6\ \mathrm{pm} = 3.306 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\).

Number of atoms in 0.5 g of niobium

\(= \dfrac{0.5\ \mathrm{g} \times 2}{8.55\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}} \times (3.306 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^3} = 3.24 \times 10^{21}\)

ii. Number of unit cells in \(x\) g \(= \dfrac{x}{\rho a^3}\)

Number of unit cells in 0.5 g of niobium

\(= \dfrac{0.5\ \mathrm{g}}{8.55\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}} \times (3.306 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^3} = 1.62 \times 10^{21}\)
note: The expression gives 3.237e21 -> 3.24e21 (as the note above says), printed 3.25e21.
